**(Section)**

Among these is His Exalted saying: ﴿By those who drag out [the souls] with violence, and by those who draw out gently, and by those who glide swiftly, and then outstrip with speed, and then arrange the affair﴾.

These are five matters, and they are the attributes of the angels. So God, glorified is He, swore by the angels performing these actions, since that is among the greatest of His signs. The object of "nazʿ" (drawing out) and "nashṭ" (drawing gently) is omitted, because if it were mentioned, saying what is drawn out and what is drawn gently, it would give the impression that the oath was restricted to that object, and that the oath was on the actions themselves as issued by these agents. Therefore the purpose was not tied to mentioning the object, as in His saying: ﴿As for him who gives and fears [God]﴾ and its like. So the drawing out itself was intended, not the thing drawn out.

Most of the exegetes hold that these are the angels who draw out the souls of the children of Adam from their bodies, and they are a group, as in His saying: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾, and His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you﴾, it is either that he is one, with helpers, or that the intended meaning is the genus rather than the singular, as in His saying: ﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾, and His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾.

"Nazʿ" is the forceful pulling of a thing. "Al-ighraq fi al-nazʿ" (exceeding in drawing out) means to draw it to its end. From this comes "ighraq al-nazʿ" in the pulling of strength, when one carries it to the furthest extent of stretching, and it is said: "He exceeded in drawing (aghraqa fi al-nazʿ)." Then it became a proverb for everyone who goes to extremes in an action until he reaches its end.

"Gharq" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the verb, just as "ʿaṭāʾ" (giving) and "kalām" (speech) are placed in the position of "iʿṭāʾ" (giving) and "takallum" (speaking).

People differed as to whether "al-nazʿāt" is transitive or intransitive. On the view we have related, it is transitive. This is the view of ʿAlī, Masrūq, Muqātil, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and ʿAṭiyya on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Masʿūd said: they are the souls of the disbelievers. This is also the view of Qatādah, al-Suddī, and ʿAṭāʾ on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās. According to this, it is intransitive, and "gharqan" (exceedingly) according to this means a drawing out that is as severe as possible and most intense.

In this view there is weakness from several aspects. First, that the conjunction of what follows it with it indicates that they are the angels: they are "al-sābiḥāt" (those who glide), "al-sābiqāt" (those who outstrip), and "al-mudabbirāt" (those who arrange), and "al-nāziʿāt" (those who draw out). Second, that swearing by the souls of the disbelievers specifically is not clear, and nothing in the wording indicates it. Third, that "nazʿ" is shared between the souls of the children of Adam, and "ighraq" is not specific to the disbeliever.

Al-Ḥasan said: "al-nāziʿāt" are the stars, which draw out from the east to the west, and "gharqan" is their setting. He said: they draw out from here and set here. This was chosen by al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayd.

Mujāhid said: they are the severities and terrors of death, which draw out the spirits with severe drawing.

ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah said: they are the bows. According to this view, "al-nāziʿāt" means in the sense of "al-nisab" (relation), or possessors of the drawing, by which the archer draws, so he is "al-nāzīʿ."

I say: "al-nāziʿāt" is the active participle from "nazaʿa." It is said: "nazaʿa kadhā" when one drags it with force; "nazaʿa ʿanhu" when one leaves it and abandons it after being engaged with it; and "nazaʿa ilayhi" when one goes toward it and toward what is near it. This attribute applies only to souls that have voluntary movement, in inclination toward a thing or away from it. The most deserving of this description are the angels, because this power is most perfect in them, and the place of the verse is greatest concerning them. They are the ones who exceed in drawing when they seek to draw out what they draw or to draw toward it. The human soul also has this power, and the stars also draw from horizon to horizon. So "nazʿ" is a violent movement, whether it comes from an angel, a human soul, or a star. Souls draw toward their homelands and their familiar places, and at death they draw toward their Lord: "the deaths draw out the souls." Bows draw with arrows, angels draw from place to place and draw what they have been charged to draw, and horses draw at their bridles, drawing so strongly that the bridles are exceeded because of the length of their necks.

So the attribute applies to everything that has this movement, which is one of the signs of the Lord, exalted is He, for it is He who created it, created its locus, and created the power and soul by which it moves. Whoever mentions one form of these forms is only giving an example, although the angels are the most deserving of this attribute.

So He swore by the groups and categories of the angels: they are "al-nāziʿāt," which draw out the spirits from the bodies; and "al-nāshiṭāt," which draw them out, that is, bring them out swiftly and lightly, from the expression "nashaṭa al-dalw min al-bi'r" (he drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out, and "anā anshaṭu bi-kadhā" (I am more nimble for such and such), meaning lighter for it and quicker. And "al-sābiḥāt" are those that glide in the air along their path of passage toward what they have been commanded, as birds glide in the air. And "al-sābiqāt" are those that outstrip and hasten toward what they have been commanded, not slow down from it nor delay. And "al-mudabbirāt" are the affairs of the servants, which their Lord has commanded them to arrange. This is the most correct of the sayings.

It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "al-nāziʿāt" are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers with severity and violence, and "al-nāshiṭāt" are the angels who draw out the spirits of the believers with ease and gentleness. Al-Farrāʾ chose this view and said: they are the angels who draw out the soul of the believer so they take it, and draw out the soul of the disbeliever.

Al-Wāḥidī said: he only chose this because of the difference between "nashṭ" and "nazʿ" in severity and gentleness. "Nazʿ" is pulling with force, and "nashṭ" is pulling with gentleness and softness. "Al-nāshiṭāt" are the souls that are quick to do what they have been commanded, and the angels are the most deserving of creatures of this, and the souls of the believers are quick to do what they have been commanded.

It was said: "al-sābiḥāt" are the stars that glide in the orbit, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. It was said: they are ships that glide on the water. It was said: they are the souls of the believers that glide after separation, ascending to their Lord.

I say: the correct view is that they are the angels, and the context indicates it.

As for ships and stars, they are called "jāriyah" (running) and "jawārī," as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾, and He said: ﴿We carried you in the running [ship]﴾, and He said: ﴿The running, disappearing [stars]﴾.

He did not name them "sābiḥāt," even though the act of gliding was applied to them, as in His saying: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. What indicates this is His mention of "al-sābiqāt" after them, and "al-mudabbirāt" with the particle "fa" (then). And His mention of the first three with "wa" (and) is because outstripping and arranging are caused by what was mentioned before them: they drew out, they glided, and they glided, so they outstripped toward what they were commanded, and so they arranged it. If "al-sābiḥāt" were ships, or stars, or human souls, then the act of outstripping and arranging would not have been joined to them with "fa." So consider this.

Masrūq, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī said: "fa al-sābiqāt sabqan" are the angels. Mujāhid and Abū Rawq said: they outstrip the son of Adam in goodness, righteous deed, faith, and belief. Muqātil said: they outstrip with the spirits of the believers to Paradise.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: they are the angels who outstrip the devils with the revelation to the prophets when the devils are eavesdropping.

This view is an error whose corruption is not hidden, because it implies that the angels and the devils share in conveying the revelation, and that the angels outstrip them with it to the prophets. This is not correct, for the revelation that the angels bring to the prophets is not eavesdropped by the devils, who are kept away from hearing it. Even if they eavesdrop on some of what they hear from the angels of the lowest heaven concerning matters of events, God, glorified is He, preserved His revelation to the prophets so that the devils could not eavesdrop anything from it, and He kept them away from hearing it.

If the proponent of this view had explained "al-sābiqāt" as the angels who outstrip the devils with the shooting stars before the devil casts the word he eavesdropped, it would have had some basis. For the devil hastens quickly to cast what he has stolen to his ally, and the angels outstrip him in descending with the piercing shooting stars and destroy him. Sometimes he casts the word before the shooting star reaches him.

"Al-sābiqāt sabqan" has also been explained as the souls that outstrip toward the obedience of God and His good pleasure.

As for "al-mudabbirāt amran," they agreed that they are the angels. Muqātil said: they are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, and the Angel of Death, who arrange the command of God in the earth; and they are "al-muqassimāt amran" (those who apportion the affair).

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sābāṭ said: Jibrīl is charged with the winds and the armies, Mīkāʾīl is charged with rain and plants, the Angel of Death is charged with taking souls, and Isrāfīl descends with the command of God to them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the angels whom God has charged with affairs, whose practice and oversight He has made known to them. Some of them are for the children of Adam, guarding and recording, and some are charged with the rains, the plants, the sinking of the earth, transformation, the winds, and the clouds. End of quotation.

He has informed us that God has charged an angel with the shooting stars, that an angel is charged with dreams, and that there are angels charged with the building of Paradise, the making of its instruments, vessels, plantings, carpets, cushions, and couches; and that there are angels charged with the work of the Fire, its kindling, and other things.

So the world and what is in it, Paradise and the Fire, death, and the rulings of the intermediate state (al-barzakh), God has charged angels with all of that, who arrange whatever God wills of it. For this reason, belief in the angels is one of the pillars of faith, without which faith is not complete.

As for the one who said they are the stars, this is not the saying of the people of Islam. God has not made the stars arrange any of the creation; rather they are arranged and subjugated, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾.

So God, glorified is He, is the Arranger through His angels of the affair of the upper and lower world.

Al-Jurjānī said: "al-sābiqāt" and "al-mudabbirāt" were mentioned with "fa," while what came before them with "wa," because what came before them were separate oaths, and these two oaths arise from what precedes them, as if He said: "then those that glided and so outstripped." Just as you say: "he stood up and then went" — the "fa" makes the standing a cause of the going. If you say "he stood and went," you have not made the standing a cause of the going.

Al-Wāḥidī objected to him, saying: this is not consistent in this verse, for it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, while the outstripping ones are not the angels according to the commentators.

I say: the angels are certainly included among the outstripping ones. As for the restriction of the outstripping ones to the angels, this is possible. And as for his saying that it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, it is not as he claimed. Rather, outstripping is hastening to carry out what the angel is commanded, so it is the cause of the act he was commanded to do, which is arranging. Moreover, "fa" indicates succession, and arranging follows outstripping without delay, unlike the three previous oaths. And God knows best.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and the context indicates it: it is the resurrection, which entails the truthfulness of the Messenger and the establishment of the Qur'an. Or it is of the type of oath intended to draw attention to the indication and the lesson in the thing sworn by, without meaning a specific sworn-to matter.

This oath includes the sworn-to answer even if it is not stated verbally.

Perhaps this is what those who said it is omitted for knowledge of it meant, but this approach is more subtle, for when the sworn-by thing indicates the sworn-to matter and entails it, it is sufficient to mention it by mentioning the sworn-by thing. This is different from it being omitted because what follows indicates it. So consider this.

Perhaps this is the view of those who said that He swore only by the Lord of these things, and the noun was omitted. Its meaning is correct, but in a way other than what they supposed, for His oath by these things is because their indication of His lordship, oneness, knowledge, power, and wisdom is manifest. So the oath by them is in reality an oath by His lordship and attributes of perfection. So consider this.

**(Section: On the fact that the upper and lower world came into being by love and for its sake, and that the movements of the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the movements of the angels and animals, and the movement of every moving thing, came into being only through the cause of love)**

This is one of the noblest chapters of the book. Before establishing it, a preface must be stated: movements are of three kinds: voluntary movement, natural movement, and forced movement. The demonstration of this division is that the origin of movement is either from the moving thing or from something other than it.

If it is from the moving thing, then either awareness and knowledge accompany it or not. If awareness and knowledge accompany it, it is voluntary. If they do not accompany it, it is natural. And if it is from something other than it, it is forced.

If you prefer to say: the moving thing either moves by its will or not. If it moves by its will, its movement is voluntary. If it moves without its will, then either its movement is toward its center or not. If it moves toward the direction of its center, its movement is natural. If it moves in a direction other than the direction of its center, its movement is forced.

Once this is established, voluntary movement follows the will of the mover. The willed thing is either willed for itself or for something else, and the willed thing for something else must end in a thing willed for itself, to avoid circularity and infinite regress. The will is either for bringing about benefit and pleasure, either for the mover or for another, or for repelling pain and harm, either from the mover or from another. The reasonable person does not bring benefit to another or repel harm from him except for what he has in that of pleasure and repelling pain. So his voluntary movement follows his love. Indeed, this is the judgment of every living moving thing.

As for natural movement, it is the movement of a thing toward its settled place and its center, and that follows the movement which required its departure from its center. That is forced movement, which occurs only by the compulsion of a compeller that removes it from its center, either by its choice, as the movement of a stone downward when it is thrown upward in a direction, or without the choice of its mover, as the moving of the winds for bodies toward the direction they blow. This movement follows the compeller, and the movement of the compeller is not from it, but its origin is from something else. For the angels are charged with the upper and lower world, arranging it by the command of God, mighty and majestic, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then those who arrange the affair﴾. He said: ﴿Then those who apportion the affair﴾. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿By those sent forth in gusts, then those that blow violently, and those that spread [clouds] widely, and then those that separate [truth from falsehood] distinctly, and then those that deliver a reminder﴾. He said: ﴿By those who drag out [the souls] with violence, and by those who draw out gently, and by those who glide swiftly, and then outstrip with speed, and then arrange the affair﴾.

God, the Exalted, has charged angels with the spheres, the sun, and the moon, who move them, and He has charged angels with the winds, who direct them by His command, and they are its guardians. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent, screaming wind﴾.

Some of the early scholars said: it raged against the guardians, so they could not control it. Al-Bukhārī mentioned this in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

He has charged angels with the rain, and angels with the clouds, who drive them wherever they are commanded. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "While a man was in a barren land of the earth, he heard a voice in a cloud saying: Water the garden of so-and-so. That cloud moved aside, emptied its water into a rocky plain, and there was a watercourse from those watercourses that had absorbed all of that water. He followed the water, and there was a man standing in his garden turning the water with his spade. He said to him: O servant of God, what is your name? He said: So-and-so, using the name he had heard in the cloud. He said to him: O servant of God, why do you ask me about my name? He said: I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is, saying: Water the garden of so-and-so, using your name. What do you do with it? He said: Since you have said this, I look at what comes out of it, and I give a third of it in charity, I and my dependents eat a third, and I return a third of it to it."

God, glorified is He, charged angels with the mountains. And it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the angel of the mountains came to him, greeted him, and asked his permission to destroy his people if he wished. He said: "Rather, I will wait for them, perhaps God will bring forth from their loins one who worships God and associates nothing with Him."

He charged an angel with the womb, who says: O Lord, a drop of semen; O Lord, a clinging clot; O Lord, a lump of flesh; O Lord, male or female? What is his provision? What is his term? Is he wretched or happy?

He charged with every servant four angels in this world: two guarding him, one on his right and one on his left, recording his deeds; and successive angels from before him and behind him, at least two, guarding him by the command of God.

He charged angels with death, and charged angels with questioning the dead in their graves.

He charged angels with mercy, and angels with punishment, and angels with the believer who strengthen him and urge him toward obedience with urging.

He charged angels with the Fire, who build it, kindle it, make its shackles and chains, and carry out its command.

He charged angels with Paradise, who build it, carpet it, and make its couches, thrones, dishes, cushions, and rugs.

Then He commanded the upper and lower worlds, and the Garden and the Fire, to be administered by the angels, by the permission of their Lord, blessed and exalted, and by His command: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ and ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾. He informed that they do not disobey Him in His command, and that they are able to carry out His orders, with no inability in them to do so, unlike one who abandons what he is commanded out of incapacity. Such a one does not disobey Allah in what He commanded him, even if he does not do what he was commanded. Likewise, the seas have been entrusted to angels who kindle them and prevent them from overflowing onto the earth and drowning its people. Likewise, the deeds of the children of Adam, good and bad, have been entrusted to angels who count them, guard them and record them. For this reason, belief in the angels is one of the pillars of faith, which is not complete without it, and it is one of the five: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day.

When this is known, it is known that every movement in the world has the angels as its cause, and their movement is obedience to Allah by His command and His will. Thus the whole matter returns to the execution of the Lord's will, both legislated and decreed, and the angels are those who execute that by His command. For this reason they were named "malāʾika" (angels), from al-ulūka (al-alūka), which means the message; they are the messengers of Allah in executing His commands.

The point is that the movements of the celestial spheres and what they contain follow the volitional movement that necessarily entails love. Love and will are the origin and source of every act, so no act occurs except from love and will. Even when one repels things he dislikes and hates, he repels them by his will and his love for their opposites, and by the pleasure he finds in repelling them, as it is said: "he cured his anger" and "he cured his chest." Healing and well-being belong to what is beloved, even if it is unpleasant, such as drinking the medicine by which the pain of illness is repelled. Although it is disliked from one aspect, it is beloved because of what it contains of removing the disliked and attaining the beloved. Likewise, doing things that oppose desire: although they are disliked, they are done out of love and will, even if they are not beloved in themselves, for they necessarily entail what is beloved in itself. A living being does not abandon what he loves and desires except for what he loves and desires, but he leaves the weaker of two loves for the stronger of two loves. For this reason love and will are the basis of hatred and aversion, since the hated and disliked contradicts the existence of the beloved. The act either seeks the existence of the beloved or the repelling of the disliked, which necessarily entails the existence of the beloved. Thus the whole act returns to the existence of the beloved.

The voluntary movement has will as its origin, while the forced and natural movements follow it. So the matter returns to voluntary movement. All movements of the upper and lower worlds follow will and love, by which the world is moved and for whose sake it moves. Thus they are the efficient and final cause; indeed, they are that by which and for which the world came into existence. No movement occurs in the upper or lower world except that will and love are its cause and its end. Indeed, the reality of love is the movement of the lover's soul toward the beloved; love is a movement without stillness. The perfection of love is worship, humility, submission and obedience to the beloved. This is the truth by which and for which the heavens and the earth, this world and the Hereafter, were created. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾, and He said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾, and He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾

The truth by which and for which creation was made is the worship of Allah alone, which is the perfection of His love, humility and submission to Him, and the requirements of His servanthood: commandment, prohibition, reward and punishment. For this reason He sent the messengers, sent down the books, and created the Garden and the Fire, and the heavens and the earth were established only with justice, which is the path of Allah upon which He is, and which is the most beloved of things to Allah, the Exalted. Allah, the Exalted, said, relating from His Prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾. So He is on a straight path in His legislation and His decree, and it is the justice by which creation, command, reward and punishment appear, and it is the truth by which and for which the heavens and the earth and what is between them were created. For this reason the believers said in their worship: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You﴾.

They declared their Lord far exalted above creating the heavens in vain, without wisdom or praiseworthy end. He, glory be to Him, is praised for these praiseworthy ends just as He is praised for His essence and attributes. The praiseworthy ends in His acts are the wisdom that He loves and is pleased with. He creates what is disliked because it necessitates what He loves, and the beloved is consequent upon it. For this reason He, glory be to Him, leaves some of what He loves because of what follows from it, the loss of a beloved greater than it or the occurrence of a disliked thing more hateful to Him than that beloved. This is like how He discourages the hearts of His enemies from believing in Him and obeying Him, because He dislikes their obedience and because by it He would lose what is more beloved to Him than it: their fighting, what follows from it of loyalty for His sake and enmity for His sake, the giving of their lives by His friends for His sake, and preferring His love and pleasure over their own souls. For this reason He created death and life and made what is on the earth an adornment for it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾.

And He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾.

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾.

So He, glory be to Him, informed that the creation of the world, death and life, and the adornment of the earth with what is upon it, is for trial and examination, to test His creatures as to which of them is best in deed. His deed then conforms to the beloved things of the Lord, the Exalted, and thus matches the end for which He created him and for which He created the world, which is His worship, which includes His love and obedience. This is the best deed, which is what meets His love and pleasure. He decreed decrees that oppose them, in His wisdom in decreeing them, and He tested His creatures between His command and His decree, that He may test them as to which of them is best in deed. Thus the creatures divided in this trial into two groups. One group moved with His commands and His beloved things, stopped where the command stopped them, moved where the command moved them, used the command within the decree, rode the ship of the command on the sea of the decree, made the command judge over the decree, and contended with the decree by the decree, in compliance with His command and following His good pleasure.

These are the ones who are saved.

The second group set the command against the decree, and what He loves and is pleased with against what He decreed and ordained.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said:

So the movements of the upper and lower worlds and what is in them conform to the command, either the religious command which Allah loves and is pleased with, or the cosmic command which He decreed and ordained. He, glory be to Him, did not decree it aimlessly nor ordain it in vain, but because of the wisdom and praiseworthy ends in it, and what follows from it of matters whose ends He loves even if He dislikes their causes and beginnings. Indeed, He, glory be to Him and exalted, loves forgiveness even though He dislikes His servants' disobedience; He loves concealing even though He dislikes what He conceals from His servant; He loves freeing slaves even though He dislikes the cause by which a servant is freed from the Fire; He loves pardon, as in the hadith: "O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me," even though He dislikes the sins He pardons; He loves those who repent and their repentance, even though He dislikes the disobedience from which they repent to Him; He loves jihad and its people, indeed they are the most beloved of His creatures to Him, even though He dislikes the actions of those who fight against Him.

This is a vast door that has been opened for you, so enter through it, and it will show you gardens of knowledge, radiant, whose fragrance whoever misses them dies of regret. And success is from Allah.

This is a matter that several journeys would not contain, and the intelligent one enters it through its gate.

The secret of this door is that He, glory be to Him, is perfect in His names and attributes. He has absolute perfection from all aspects, with no deficiency in any way. He loves His names and attributes and loves the manifestation of their effects in His creatures, for that is among the requirements of His perfection. He, glory be to Him, is Witr (the One), and He loves the odd; He is Jamil (Beautiful) and He loves beauty; He is 'Alim (Knowing) and He loves the scholars; He is Jawad (Generous) and He loves the generous; He is Qawi (Strong), and the strong believer is more beloved to Him than the weak believer; He is Hayy (Modest), and He loves those who are modest; He is Wafi (Faithful), and He loves those who are faithful; He is Shakur (Appreciative), and He loves the grateful; He is Sadiq (Truthful), and He loves the truthful; He is Muhsin (Good-doer), and He loves the good-doers.

So if He loves pardon, forgiveness, forbearance, overlooking and concealment, there must be His decreeing the causes in which the effects of these attributes appear, by which He makes His servants aware of His names and attributes. That is more conducive to their love of Him, their praise of Him, their glorifying Him and their extolling Him with what is worthy of Him. Thus the purpose for which creation was made is achieved. If it is missed in some of them, that is because of the loss of a cause for its perfection and manifestation; that loss, though disliked by Him, entails something He loves more than its absence. So contemplate this point with true contemplation. This will be fully revealed on the Day of Resurrection to all the creatures, when He gathers them in one plain, and delivers to every soul what should be delivered to it of good and evil, pleasure and pain, down to the weight of an atom, and brings every soul to its ends, which it itself will testify that it deserves. Then the whole universe will speak His praise, blessed and exalted, both in words and in state, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with praise of their Lord. And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said, "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

The subject of the saying is omitted because it is not specified; rather, everyone praises Him for that judgment which He has passed. The people of the heavens and the people of the earth praise Him, the righteous and the wicked, humans and jinn, even the people of the Fire.

Al-Hasan or someone else said: "They will have entered the Fire, and yet the praise of Him will be in their hearts, which they will find no way to avoid."

This, and Allah knows best, is the secret for which the subject is omitted in His saying: ﴿It will be said, "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein"﴾, and His saying: ﴿And it will be said, "Enter the Fire with those who enter."﴾ As if the whole universe speaks that and says it to them. And Allah knows best what is correct.

**(Section)**

Among these is His Exalted saying: ﴿By those who drag out [the souls] with violence, and by those who draw out gently, and by those who glide swiftly, and then outstrip with speed, and then arrange the affair﴾.

These are five matters, and they are the attributes of the angels. So God, glorified is He, swore by the angels performing these actions, since that is among the greatest of His signs. The object of "nazʿ" (drawing out) and "nashṭ" (drawing gently) is omitted, because if it were mentioned, saying what is drawn out and what is drawn gently, it would give the impression that the oath was restricted to that object, and that the oath was on the actions themselves as issued by these agents. Therefore the purpose was not tied to mentioning the object, as in His saying: ﴿As for him who gives and fears [God]﴾ and its like. So the drawing out itself was intended, not the thing drawn out.

Most of the exegetes hold that these are the angels who draw out the souls of the children of Adam from their bodies, and they are a group, as in His saying: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾, and His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you﴾, it is either that he is one, with helpers, or that the intended meaning is the genus rather than the singular, as in His saying: ﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾, and His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾.

"Nazʿ" is the forceful pulling of a thing. "Al-ighraq fi al-nazʿ" (exceeding in drawing out) means to draw it to its end. From this comes "ighraq al-nazʿ" in the pulling of strength, when one carries it to the furthest extent of stretching, and it is said: "He exceeded in drawing (aghraqa fi al-nazʿ)." Then it became a proverb for everyone who goes to extremes in an action until he reaches its end.

"Gharq" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the verb, just as "ʿaṭāʾ" (giving) and "kalām" (speech) are placed in the position of "iʿṭāʾ" (giving) and "takallum" (speaking).

People differed as to whether "al-nazʿāt" is transitive or intransitive. On the view we have related, it is transitive. This is the view of ʿAlī, Masrūq, Muqātil, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and ʿAṭiyya on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Masʿūd said: they are the souls of the disbelievers. This is also the view of Qatādah, al-Suddī, and ʿAṭāʾ on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās. According to this, it is intransitive, and "gharqan" (exceedingly) according to this means a drawing out that is as severe as possible and most intense.

In this view there is weakness from several aspects. First, that the conjunction of what follows it with it indicates that they are the angels: they are "al-sābiḥāt" (those who glide), "al-sābiqāt" (those who outstrip), and "al-mudabbirāt" (those who arrange), and "al-nāziʿāt" (those who draw out). Second, that swearing by the souls of the disbelievers specifically is not clear, and nothing in the wording indicates it. Third, that "nazʿ" is shared between the souls of the children of Adam, and "ighraq" is not specific to the disbeliever.

Al-Ḥasan said: "al-nāziʿāt" are the stars, which draw out from the east to the west, and "gharqan" is their setting. He said: they draw out from here and set here. This was chosen by al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayd.

Mujāhid said: they are the severities and terrors of death, which draw out the spirits with severe drawing.

ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah said: they are the bows. According to this view, "al-nāziʿāt" means in the sense of "al-nisab" (relation), or possessors of the drawing, by which the archer draws, so he is "al-nāzīʿ."

I say: "al-nāziʿāt" is the active participle from "nazaʿa." It is said: "nazaʿa kadhā" when one drags it with force; "nazaʿa ʿanhu" when one leaves it and abandons it after being engaged with it; and "nazaʿa ilayhi" when one goes toward it and toward what is near it. This attribute applies only to souls that have voluntary movement, in inclination toward a thing or away from it. The most deserving of this description are the angels, because this power is most perfect in them, and the place of the verse is greatest concerning them. They are the ones who exceed in drawing when they seek to draw out what they draw or to draw toward it. The human soul also has this power, and the stars also draw from horizon to horizon. So "nazʿ" is a violent movement, whether it comes from an angel, a human soul, or a star. Souls draw toward their homelands and their familiar places, and at death they draw toward their Lord: "the deaths draw out the souls." Bows draw with arrows, angels draw from place to place and draw what they have been charged to draw, and horses draw at their bridles, drawing so strongly that the bridles are exceeded because of the length of their necks.

So the attribute applies to everything that has this movement, which is one of the signs of the Lord, exalted is He, for it is He who created it, created its locus, and created the power and soul by which it moves. Whoever mentions one form of these forms is only giving an example, although the angels are the most deserving of this attribute.

So He swore by the groups and categories of the angels: they are "al-nāziʿāt," which draw out the spirits from the bodies; and "al-nāshiṭāt," which draw them out, that is, bring them out swiftly and lightly, from the expression "nashaṭa al-dalw min al-bi'r" (he drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out, and "anā anshaṭu bi-kadhā" (I am more nimble for such and such), meaning lighter for it and quicker. And "al-sābiḥāt" are those that glide in the air along their path of passage toward what they have been commanded, as birds glide in the air. And "al-sābiqāt" are those that outstrip and hasten toward what they have been commanded, not slow down from it nor delay. And "al-mudabbirāt" are the affairs of the servants, which their Lord has commanded them to arrange. This is the most correct of the sayings.

It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "al-nāziʿāt" are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers with severity and violence, and "al-nāshiṭāt" are the angels who draw out the spirits of the believers with ease and gentleness. Al-Farrāʾ chose this view and said: they are the angels who draw out the soul of the believer so they take it, and draw out the soul of the disbeliever.

Al-Wāḥidī said: he only chose this because of the difference between "nashṭ" and "nazʿ" in severity and gentleness. "Nazʿ" is pulling with force, and "nashṭ" is pulling with gentleness and softness. "Al-nāshiṭāt" are the souls that are quick to do what they have been commanded, and the angels are the most deserving of creatures of this, and the souls of the believers are quick to do what they have been commanded.

It was said: "al-sābiḥāt" are the stars that glide in the orbit, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. It was said: they are ships that glide on the water. It was said: they are the souls of the believers that glide after separation, ascending to their Lord.

I say: the correct view is that they are the angels, and the context indicates it.

As for ships and stars, they are called "jāriyah" (running) and "jawārī," as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾, and He said: ﴿We carried you in the running [ship]﴾, and He said: ﴿The running, disappearing [stars]﴾.

He did not name them "sābiḥāt," even though the act of gliding was applied to them, as in His saying: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. What indicates this is His mention of "al-sābiqāt" after them, and "al-mudabbirāt" with the particle "fa" (then). And His mention of the first three with "wa" (and) is because outstripping and arranging are caused by what was mentioned before them: they drew out, they glided, and they glided, so they outstripped toward what they were commanded, and so they arranged it. If "al-sābiḥāt" were ships, or stars, or human souls, then the act of outstripping and arranging would not have been joined to them with "fa." So consider this.

Masrūq, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī said: "fa al-sābiqāt sabqan" are the angels. Mujāhid and Abū Rawq said: they outstrip the son of Adam in goodness, righteous deed, faith, and belief. Muqātil said: they outstrip with the spirits of the believers to Paradise.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: they are the angels who outstrip the devils with the revelation to the prophets when the devils are eavesdropping.

This view is an error whose corruption is not hidden, because it implies that the angels and the devils share in conveying the revelation, and that the angels outstrip them with it to the prophets. This is not correct, for the revelation that the angels bring to the prophets is not eavesdropped by the devils, who are kept away from hearing it. Even if they eavesdrop on some of what they hear from the angels of the lowest heaven concerning matters of events, God, glorified is He, preserved His revelation to the prophets so that the devils could not eavesdrop anything from it, and He kept them away from hearing it.

If the proponent of this view had explained "al-sābiqāt" as the angels who outstrip the devils with the shooting stars before the devil casts the word he eavesdropped, it would have had some basis. For the devil hastens quickly to cast what he has stolen to his ally, and the angels outstrip him in descending with the piercing shooting stars and destroy him. Sometimes he casts the word before the shooting star reaches him.

"Al-sābiqāt sabqan" has also been explained as the souls that outstrip toward the obedience of God and His good pleasure.

As for "al-mudabbirāt amran," they agreed that they are the angels. Muqātil said: they are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, and the Angel of Death, who arrange the command of God in the earth; and they are "al-muqassimāt amran" (those who apportion the affair).

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sābāṭ said: Jibrīl is charged with the winds and the armies, Mīkāʾīl is charged with rain and plants, the Angel of Death is charged with taking souls, and Isrāfīl descends with the command of God to them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the angels whom God has charged with affairs, whose practice and oversight He has made known to them. Some of them are for the children of Adam, guarding and recording, and some are charged with the rains, the plants, the sinking of the earth, transformation, the winds, and the clouds. End of quotation.

He has informed us that God has charged an angel with the shooting stars, that an angel is charged with dreams, and that there are angels charged with the building of Paradise, the making of its instruments, vessels, plantings, carpets, cushions, and couches; and that there are angels charged with the work of the Fire, its kindling, and other things.

So the world and what is in it, Paradise and the Fire, death, and the rulings of the intermediate state (al-barzakh), God has charged angels with all of that, who arrange whatever God wills of it. For this reason, belief in the angels is one of the pillars of faith, without which faith is not complete.

As for the one who said they are the stars, this is not the saying of the people of Islam. God has not made the stars arrange any of the creation; rather they are arranged and subjugated, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾.

So God, glorified is He, is the Arranger through His angels of the affair of the upper and lower world.

Al-Jurjānī said: "al-sābiqāt" and "al-mudabbirāt" were mentioned with "fa," while what came before them with "wa," because what came before them were separate oaths, and these two oaths arise from what precedes them, as if He said: "then those that glided and so outstripped." Just as you say: "he stood up and then went" — the "fa" makes the standing a cause of the going. If you say "he stood and went," you have not made the standing a cause of the going.

Al-Wāḥidī objected to him, saying: this is not consistent in this verse, for it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, while the outstripping ones are not the angels according to the commentators.

I say: the angels are certainly included among the outstripping ones. As for the restriction of the outstripping ones to the angels, this is possible. And as for his saying that it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, it is not as he claimed. Rather, outstripping is hastening to carry out what the angel is commanded, so it is the cause of the act he was commanded to do, which is arranging. Moreover, "fa" indicates succession, and arranging follows outstripping without delay, unlike the three previous oaths. And God knows best.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and the context indicates it: it is the resurrection, which entails the truthfulness of the Messenger and the establishment of the Qur'an. Or it is of the type of oath intended to draw attention to the indication and the lesson in the thing sworn by, without meaning a specific sworn-to matter.

This oath includes the sworn-to answer even if it is not stated verbally.

Perhaps this is what those who said it is omitted for knowledge of it meant, but this approach is more subtle, for when the sworn-by thing indicates the sworn-to matter and entails it, it is sufficient to mention it by mentioning the sworn-by thing. This is different from it being omitted because what follows indicates it. So consider this.

Perhaps this is the view of those who said that He swore only by the Lord of these things, and the noun was omitted. Its meaning is correct, but in a way other than what they supposed, for His oath by these things is because their indication of His lordship, oneness, knowledge, power, and wisdom is manifest. So the oath by them is in reality an oath by His lordship and attributes of perfection. So consider this.

**(Section: On the fact that the upper and lower world came into being by love and for its sake, and that the movements of the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the movements of the angels and animals, and the movement of every moving thing, came into being only through the cause of love)**

This is one of the noblest chapters of the book. Before establishing it, a preface must be stated: movements are of three kinds: voluntary movement, natural movement, and forced movement. The demonstration of this division is that the origin of movement is either from the moving thing or from something other than it.

If it is from the moving thing, then either awareness and knowledge accompany it or not. If awareness and knowledge accompany it, it is voluntary. If they do not accompany it, it is natural. And if it is from something other than it, it is forced.

If you prefer to say: the moving thing either moves by its will or not. If it moves by its will, its movement is voluntary. If it moves without its will, then either its movement is toward its center or not. If it moves toward the direction of its center, its movement is natural. If it moves in a direction other than the direction of its center, its movement is forced.

Once this is established, voluntary movement follows the will of the mover. The willed thing is either willed for itself or for something else, and the willed thing for something else must end in a thing willed for itself, to avoid circularity and infinite regress. The will is either for bringing about benefit and pleasure, either for the mover or for another, or for repelling pain and harm, either from the mover or from another. The reasonable person does not bring benefit to another or repel harm from him except for what he has in that of pleasure and repelling pain. So his voluntary movement follows his love. Indeed, this is the judgment of every living moving thing.

As for natural movement, it is the movement of a thing toward its settled place and its center, and that follows the movement which required its departure from its center. That is forced movement, which occurs only by the compulsion of a compeller that removes it from its center, either by its choice, as the movement of a stone downward when it is thrown upward in a direction, or without the choice of its mover, as the moving of the winds for bodies toward the direction they blow. This movement follows the compeller, and the movement of the compeller is not from it, but its origin is from something else. For the angels are charged with the upper and lower world, arranging it by the command of God, mighty and majestic, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then those who arrange the affair﴾. He said: ﴿Then those who apportion the affair﴾. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿By those sent forth in gusts, then those that blow violently, and those that spread [clouds] widely, and then those that separate [truth from falsehood] distinctly, and then those that deliver a reminder﴾. He said: ﴿By those who drag out [the souls] with violence, and by those who draw out gently, and by those who glide swiftly, and then outstrip with speed, and then arrange the affair﴾.

God, the Exalted, has charged angels with the spheres, the sun, and the moon, who move them, and He has charged angels with the winds, who direct them by His command, and they are its guardians. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent, screaming wind﴾.

Some of the early scholars said: it raged against the guardians, so they could not control it. Al-Bukhārī mentioned this in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

He has charged angels with the rain, and angels with the clouds, who drive them wherever they are commanded. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "While a man was in a barren land of the earth, he heard a voice in a cloud saying: Water the garden of so-and-so. That cloud moved aside, emptied its water into a rocky plain, and there was a watercourse from those watercourses that had absorbed all of that water. He followed the water, and there was a man standing in his garden turning the water with his spade. He said to him: O servant of God, what is your name? He said: So-and-so, using the name he had heard in the cloud. He said to him: O servant of God, why do you ask me about my name? He said: I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is, saying: Water the garden of so-and-so, using your name. What do you do with it? He said: Since you have said this, I look at what comes out of it, and I give a third of it in charity, I and my dependents eat a third, and I return a third of it to it."

God, glorified is He, charged angels with the mountains. And it is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the angel of the mountains came to him, greeted him, and asked his permission to destroy his people if he wished. He said: "Rather, I will wait for them, perhaps God will bring forth from their loins one who worships God and associates nothing with Him."

He charged an angel with the womb, who says: O Lord, a drop of semen; O Lord, a clinging clot; O Lord, a lump of flesh; O Lord, male or female? What is his provision? What is his term? Is he wretched or happy?

He charged with every servant four angels in this world: two guarding him, one on his right and one on his left, recording his deeds; and successive angels from before him and behind him, at least two, guarding him by the command of God.

He charged angels with death, and charged angels with questioning the dead in their graves.

He charged angels with mercy, and angels with punishment, and angels with the believer who strengthen him and urge him toward obedience with urging.

He charged angels with the Fire, who build it, kindle it, make its shackles and chains, and carry out its command.

He charged angels with Paradise, who build it, carpet it, and make its couches, thrones, dishes, cushions, and rugs.

Then He commanded the upper and lower worlds, and the Garden and the Fire, to be administered by the angels, by the permission of their Lord, blessed and exalted, and by His command: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ and ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾. He informed that they do not disobey Him in His command, and that they are able to carry out His orders, with no inability in them to do so, unlike one who abandons what he is commanded out of incapacity. Such a one does not disobey Allah in what He commanded him, even if he does not do what he was commanded. Likewise, the seas have been entrusted to angels who kindle them and prevent them from overflowing onto the earth and drowning its people. Likewise, the deeds of the children of Adam, good and bad, have been entrusted to angels who count them, guard them and record them. For this reason, belief in the angels is one of the pillars of faith, which is not complete without it, and it is one of the five: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day.

When this is known, it is known that every movement in the world has the angels as its cause, and their movement is obedience to Allah by His command and His will. Thus the whole matter returns to the execution of the Lord's will, both legislated and decreed, and the angels are those who execute that by His command. For this reason they were named "malāʾika" (angels), from al-ulūka (al-alūka), which means the message; they are the messengers of Allah in executing His commands.

The point is that the movements of the celestial spheres and what they contain follow the volitional movement that necessarily entails love. Love and will are the origin and source of every act, so no act occurs except from love and will. Even when one repels things he dislikes and hates, he repels them by his will and his love for their opposites, and by the pleasure he finds in repelling them, as it is said: "he cured his anger" and "he cured his chest." Healing and well-being belong to what is beloved, even if it is unpleasant, such as drinking the medicine by which the pain of illness is repelled. Although it is disliked from one aspect, it is beloved because of what it contains of removing the disliked and attaining the beloved. Likewise, doing things that oppose desire: although they are disliked, they are done out of love and will, even if they are not beloved in themselves, for they necessarily entail what is beloved in itself. A living being does not abandon what he loves and desires except for what he loves and desires, but he leaves the weaker of two loves for the stronger of two loves. For this reason love and will are the basis of hatred and aversion, since the hated and disliked contradicts the existence of the beloved. The act either seeks the existence of the beloved or the repelling of the disliked, which necessarily entails the existence of the beloved. Thus the whole act returns to the existence of the beloved.

The voluntary movement has will as its origin, while the forced and natural movements follow it. So the matter returns to voluntary movement. All movements of the upper and lower worlds follow will and love, by which the world is moved and for whose sake it moves. Thus they are the efficient and final cause; indeed, they are that by which and for which the world came into existence. No movement occurs in the upper or lower world except that will and love are its cause and its end. Indeed, the reality of love is the movement of the lover's soul toward the beloved; love is a movement without stillness. The perfection of love is worship, humility, submission and obedience to the beloved. This is the truth by which and for which the heavens and the earth, this world and the Hereafter, were created. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾, and He said: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾, and He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾

The truth by which and for which creation was made is the worship of Allah alone, which is the perfection of His love, humility and submission to Him, and the requirements of His servanthood: commandment, prohibition, reward and punishment. For this reason He sent the messengers, sent down the books, and created the Garden and the Fire, and the heavens and the earth were established only with justice, which is the path of Allah upon which He is, and which is the most beloved of things to Allah, the Exalted. Allah, the Exalted, said, relating from His Prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾. So He is on a straight path in His legislation and His decree, and it is the justice by which creation, command, reward and punishment appear, and it is the truth by which and for which the heavens and the earth and what is between them were created. For this reason the believers said in their worship: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You﴾.

They declared their Lord far exalted above creating the heavens in vain, without wisdom or praiseworthy end. He, glory be to Him, is praised for these praiseworthy ends just as He is praised for His essence and attributes. The praiseworthy ends in His acts are the wisdom that He loves and is pleased with. He creates what is disliked because it necessitates what He loves, and the beloved is consequent upon it. For this reason He, glory be to Him, leaves some of what He loves because of what follows from it, the loss of a beloved greater than it or the occurrence of a disliked thing more hateful to Him than that beloved. This is like how He discourages the hearts of His enemies from believing in Him and obeying Him, because He dislikes their obedience and because by it He would lose what is more beloved to Him than it: their fighting, what follows from it of loyalty for His sake and enmity for His sake, the giving of their lives by His friends for His sake, and preferring His love and pleasure over their own souls. For this reason He created death and life and made what is on the earth an adornment for it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾.

And He said: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾.

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾.

So He, glory be to Him, informed that the creation of the world, death and life, and the adornment of the earth with what is upon it, is for trial and examination, to test His creatures as to which of them is best in deed. His deed then conforms to the beloved things of the Lord, the Exalted, and thus matches the end for which He created him and for which He created the world, which is His worship, which includes His love and obedience. This is the best deed, which is what meets His love and pleasure. He decreed decrees that oppose them, in His wisdom in decreeing them, and He tested His creatures between His command and His decree, that He may test them as to which of them is best in deed. Thus the creatures divided in this trial into two groups. One group moved with His commands and His beloved things, stopped where the command stopped them, moved where the command moved them, used the command within the decree, rode the ship of the command on the sea of the decree, made the command judge over the decree, and contended with the decree by the decree, in compliance with His command and following His good pleasure.

These are the ones who are saved.

The second group set the command against the decree, and what He loves and is pleased with against what He decreed and ordained.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said:

So the movements of the upper and lower worlds and what is in them conform to the command, either the religious command which Allah loves and is pleased with, or the cosmic command which He decreed and ordained. He, glory be to Him, did not decree it aimlessly nor ordain it in vain, but because of the wisdom and praiseworthy ends in it, and what follows from it of matters whose ends He loves even if He dislikes their causes and beginnings. Indeed, He, glory be to Him and exalted, loves forgiveness even though He dislikes His servants' disobedience; He loves concealing even though He dislikes what He conceals from His servant; He loves freeing slaves even though He dislikes the cause by which a servant is freed from the Fire; He loves pardon, as in the hadith: "O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me," even though He dislikes the sins He pardons; He loves those who repent and their repentance, even though He dislikes the disobedience from which they repent to Him; He loves jihad and its people, indeed they are the most beloved of His creatures to Him, even though He dislikes the actions of those who fight against Him.

This is a vast door that has been opened for you, so enter through it, and it will show you gardens of knowledge, radiant, whose fragrance whoever misses them dies of regret. And success is from Allah.

This is a matter that several journeys would not contain, and the intelligent one enters it through its gate.

The secret of this door is that He, glory be to Him, is perfect in His names and attributes. He has absolute perfection from all aspects, with no deficiency in any way. He loves His names and attributes and loves the manifestation of their effects in His creatures, for that is among the requirements of His perfection. He, glory be to Him, is Witr (the One), and He loves the odd; He is Jamil (Beautiful) and He loves beauty; He is 'Alim (Knowing) and He loves the scholars; He is Jawad (Generous) and He loves the generous; He is Qawi (Strong), and the strong believer is more beloved to Him than the weak believer; He is Hayy (Modest), and He loves those who are modest; He is Wafi (Faithful), and He loves those who are faithful; He is Shakur (Appreciative), and He loves the grateful; He is Sadiq (Truthful), and He loves the truthful; He is Muhsin (Good-doer), and He loves the good-doers.

So if He loves pardon, forgiveness, forbearance, overlooking and concealment, there must be His decreeing the causes in which the effects of these attributes appear, by which He makes His servants aware of His names and attributes. That is more conducive to their love of Him, their praise of Him, their glorifying Him and their extolling Him with what is worthy of Him. Thus the purpose for which creation was made is achieved. If it is missed in some of them, that is because of the loss of a cause for its perfection and manifestation; that loss, though disliked by Him, entails something He loves more than its absence. So contemplate this point with true contemplation. This will be fully revealed on the Day of Resurrection to all the creatures, when He gathers them in one plain, and delivers to every soul what should be delivered to it of good and evil, pleasure and pain, down to the weight of an atom, and brings every soul to its ends, which it itself will testify that it deserves. Then the whole universe will speak His praise, blessed and exalted, both in words and in state, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with praise of their Lord. And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said, "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

The subject of the saying is omitted because it is not specified; rather, everyone praises Him for that judgment which He has passed. The people of the heavens and the people of the earth praise Him, the righteous and the wicked, humans and jinn, even the people of the Fire.

Al-Hasan or someone else said: "They will have entered the Fire, and yet the praise of Him will be in their hearts, which they will find no way to avoid."

This, and Allah knows best, is the secret for which the subject is omitted in His saying: ﴿It will be said, "Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein"﴾, and His saying: ﴿And it will be said, "Enter the Fire with those who enter."﴾ As if the whole universe speaks that and says it to them. And Allah knows best what is correct.

**(Section)**

Among these is His Exalted saying: ﴿By those who drag out [the souls] with violence, and by those who draw out gently, and by those who glide swiftly, and then outstrip with speed, and then arrange the affair﴾.

These are five matters, and they are the attributes of the angels. So God, glorified is He, swore by the angels performing these actions, since that is among the greatest of His signs. The object of "nazʿ" (drawing out) and "nashṭ" (drawing gently) is omitted, because if it were mentioned, saying what is drawn out and what is drawn gently, it would give the impression that the oath was restricted to that object, and that the oath was on the actions themselves as issued by these agents. Therefore the purpose was not tied to mentioning the object, as in His saying: ﴿As for him who gives and fears [God]﴾ and its like. So the drawing out itself was intended, not the thing drawn out.

Most of the exegetes hold that these are the angels who draw out the souls of the children of Adam from their bodies, and they are a group, as in His saying: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾, and His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take you﴾, it is either that he is one, with helpers, or that the intended meaning is the genus rather than the singular, as in His saying: ﴿And she confirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures﴾, and His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favour of God, you could not enumerate it﴾.

"Nazʿ" is the forceful pulling of a thing. "Al-ighraq fi al-nazʿ" (exceeding in drawing out) means to draw it to its end. From this comes "ighraq al-nazʿ" in the pulling of strength, when one carries it to the furthest extent of stretching, and it is said: "He exceeded in drawing (aghraqa fi al-nazʿ)." Then it became a proverb for everyone who goes to extremes in an action until he reaches its end.

"Gharq" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the verb, just as "ʿaṭāʾ" (giving) and "kalām" (speech) are placed in the position of "iʿṭāʾ" (giving) and "takallum" (speaking).

People differed as to whether "al-nazʿāt" is transitive or intransitive. On the view we have related, it is transitive. This is the view of ʿAlī, Masrūq, Muqātil, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and ʿAṭiyya on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Masʿūd said: they are the souls of the disbelievers. This is also the view of Qatādah, al-Suddī, and ʿAṭāʾ on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās. According to this, it is intransitive, and "gharqan" (exceedingly) according to this means a drawing out that is as severe as possible and most intense.

In this view there is weakness from several aspects. First, that the conjunction of what follows it with it indicates that they are the angels: they are "al-sābiḥāt" (those who glide), "al-sābiqāt" (those who outstrip), and "al-mudabbirāt" (those who arrange), and "al-nāziʿāt" (those who draw out). Second, that swearing by the souls of the disbelievers specifically is not clear, and nothing in the wording indicates it. Third, that "nazʿ" is shared between the souls of the children of Adam, and "ighraq" is not specific to the disbeliever.

Al-Ḥasan said: "al-nāziʿāt" are the stars, which draw out from the east to the west, and "gharqan" is their setting. He said: they draw out from here and set here. This was chosen by al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayd.

Mujāhid said: they are the severities and terrors of death, which draw out the spirits with severe drawing.

ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrimah said: they are the bows. According to this view, "al-nāziʿāt" means in the sense of "al-nisab" (relation), or possessors of the drawing, by which the archer draws, so he is "al-nāzīʿ."

I say: "al-nāziʿāt" is the active participle from "nazaʿa." It is said: "nazaʿa kadhā" when one drags it with force; "nazaʿa ʿanhu" when one leaves it and abandons it after being engaged with it; and "nazaʿa ilayhi" when one goes toward it and toward what is near it. This attribute applies only to souls that have voluntary movement, in inclination toward a thing or away from it. The most deserving of this description are the angels, because this power is most perfect in them, and the place of the verse is greatest concerning them. They are the ones who exceed in drawing when they seek to draw out what they draw or to draw toward it. The human soul also has this power, and the stars also draw from horizon to horizon. So "nazʿ" is a violent movement, whether it comes from an angel, a human soul, or a star. Souls draw toward their homelands and their familiar places, and at death they draw toward their Lord: "the deaths draw out the souls." Bows draw with arrows, angels draw from place to place and draw what they have been charged to draw, and horses draw at their bridles, drawing so strongly that the bridles are exceeded because of the length of their necks.

So the attribute applies to everything that has this movement, which is one of the signs of the Lord, exalted is He, for it is He who created it, created its locus, and created the power and soul by which it moves. Whoever mentions one form of these forms is only giving an example, although the angels are the most deserving of this attribute.

So He swore by the groups and categories of the angels: they are "al-nāziʿāt," which draw out the spirits from the bodies; and "al-nāshiṭāt," which draw them out, that is, bring them out swiftly and lightly, from the expression "nashaṭa al-dalw min al-bi'r" (he drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out, and "anā anshaṭu bi-kadhā" (I am more nimble for such and such), meaning lighter for it and quicker. And "al-sābiḥāt" are those that glide in the air along their path of passage toward what they have been commanded, as birds glide in the air. And "al-sābiqāt" are those that outstrip and hasten toward what they have been commanded, not slow down from it nor delay. And "al-mudabbirāt" are the affairs of the servants, which their Lord has commanded them to arrange. This is the most correct of the sayings.

It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "al-nāziʿāt" are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers with severity and violence, and "al-nāshiṭāt" are the angels who draw out the spirits of the believers with ease and gentleness. Al-Farrāʾ chose this view and said: they are the angels who draw out the soul of the believer so they take it, and draw out the soul of the disbeliever.

Al-Wāḥidī said: he only chose this because of the difference between "nashṭ" and "nazʿ" in severity and gentleness. "Nazʿ" is pulling with force, and "nashṭ" is pulling with gentleness and softness. "Al-nāshiṭāt" are the souls that are quick to do what they have been commanded, and the angels are the most deserving of creatures of this, and the souls of the believers are quick to do what they have been commanded.

It was said: "al-sābiḥāt" are the stars that glide in the orbit, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. It was said: they are ships that glide on the water. It was said: they are the souls of the believers that glide after separation, ascending to their Lord.

I say: the correct view is that they are the angels, and the context indicates it.

As for ships and stars, they are called "jāriyah" (running) and "jawārī," as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains﴾, and He said: ﴿We carried you in the running [ship]﴾, and He said: ﴿The running, disappearing [stars]﴾.

He did not name them "sābiḥāt," even though the act of gliding was applied to them, as in His saying: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾. What indicates this is His mention of "al-sābiqāt" after them, and "al-mudabbirāt" with the particle "fa" (then). And His mention of the first three with "wa" (and) is because outstripping and arranging are caused by what was mentioned before them: they drew out, they glided, and they glided, so they outstripped toward what they were commanded, and so they arranged it. If "al-sābiḥāt" were ships, or stars, or human souls, then the act of outstripping and arranging would not have been joined to them with "fa." So consider this.

Masrūq, Muqātil, and al-Kalbī said: "fa al-sābiqāt sabqan" are the angels. Mujāhid and Abū Rawq said: they outstrip the son of Adam in goodness, righteous deed, faith, and belief. Muqātil said: they outstrip with the spirits of the believers to Paradise.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj said: they are the angels who outstrip the devils with the revelation to the prophets when the devils are eavesdropping.

This view is an error whose corruption is not hidden, because it implies that the angels and the devils share in conveying the revelation, and that the angels outstrip them with it to the prophets. This is not correct, for the revelation that the angels bring to the prophets is not eavesdropped by the devils, who are kept away from hearing it. Even if they eavesdrop on some of what they hear from the angels of the lowest heaven concerning matters of events, God, glorified is He, preserved His revelation to the prophets so that the devils could not eavesdrop anything from it, and He kept them away from hearing it.

If the proponent of this view had explained "al-sābiqāt" as the angels who outstrip the devils with the shooting stars before the devil casts the word he eavesdropped, it would have had some basis. For the devil hastens quickly to cast what he has stolen to his ally, and the angels outstrip him in descending with the piercing shooting stars and destroy him. Sometimes he casts the word before the shooting star reaches him.

"Al-sābiqāt sabqan" has also been explained as the souls that outstrip toward the obedience of God and His good pleasure.

As for "al-mudabbirāt amran," they agreed that they are the angels. Muqātil said: they are Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, and the Angel of Death, who arrange the command of God in the earth; and they are "al-muqassimāt amran" (those who apportion the affair).

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sābāṭ said: Jibrīl is charged with the winds and the armies, Mīkāʾīl is charged with rain and plants, the Angel of Death is charged with taking souls, and Isrāfīl descends with the command of God to them.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the angels whom God has charged with affairs, whose practice and oversight He has made known to them. Some of them are for the children of Adam, guarding and recording, and some are charged with the rains, the plants, the sinking of the earth, transformation, the winds, and the clouds. End of quotation.

He has informed us that God has charged an angel with the shooting stars, that an angel is charged with dreams, and that there are angels charged with the building of Paradise, the making of its instruments, vessels, plantings, carpets, cushions, and couches; and that there are angels charged with the work of the Fire, its kindling, and other things.

So the world and what is in it, Paradise and the Fire, death, and the rulings of the intermediate state (al-barzakh), God has charged angels with all of that, who arrange whatever God wills of it. For this reason, belief in the angels is one of the pillars of faith, without which faith is not complete.

As for the one who said they are the stars, this is not the saying of the people of Islam. God has not made the stars arrange any of the creation; rather they are arranged and subjugated, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾.

So God, glorified is He, is the Arranger through His angels of the affair of the upper and lower world.

Al-Jurjānī said: "al-sābiqāt" and "al-mudabbirāt" were mentioned with "fa," while what came before them with "wa," because what came before them were separate oaths, and these two oaths arise from what precedes them, as if He said: "then those that glided and so outstripped." Just as you say: "he stood up and then went" — the "fa" makes the standing a cause of the going. If you say "he stood and went," you have not made the standing a cause of the going.

Al-Wāḥidī objected to him, saying: this is not consistent in this verse, for it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, while the outstripping ones are not the angels according to the commentators.

I say: the angels are certainly included among the outstripping ones. As for the restriction of the outstripping ones to the angels, this is possible. And as for his saying that it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of the arranging, it is not as he claimed. Rather, outstripping is hastening to carry out what the angel is commanded, so it is the cause of the act he was commanded to do, which is arranging. Moreover, "fa" indicates succession, and arranging follows outstripping without delay, unlike the three previous oaths. And God knows best.

The answer to the oath is omitted, and the context indicates it: it is the resurrection, which entails the truthfulness of the Messenger and the establishment of the Qur'an. Or it is of the type of oath intended to draw attention to the indication and the lesson in the thing sworn by, without meaning a specific sworn-to matter.

This oath includes the sworn-to answer even if it is not stated verbally.

Perhaps this is what those who said it is omitted for knowledge of it meant, but this approach is more subtle, for when the sworn-by thing indicates the sworn-to matter and entails it, it is sufficient to mention it by mentioning the sworn-by thing. This is different from it being omitted because what follows indicates it. So consider this.

Perhaps this is the view of those who said that He swore only by the Lord of these things, and the noun was omitted. Its meaning is correct, but in a way other than what they supposed, for His oath by these things is because their indication of His lordship, oneness, knowledge, power, and wisdom is manifest. So the oath by them is in reality an oath by His lordship and attributes of perfection. So consider this.

**(Section: On the fact that the upper and lower world came into being by love and for its sake, and that the movements of the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and the movements of the angels and animals, and the movement of every moving thing, came into being only through the cause of love)**

This is one of the noblest chapters of the book. Before establishing it, a preface must be stated: movements are of three kinds: voluntary movement, natural movement, and forced movement. The demonstration of this division is that the origin of movement is either from the moving thing or from something other than it.
