Thus it is at rest in Him alone as its Lord, its God, its object of worship, its King, and the owner of its entire affair, and that its return is to Him, and that it has no need of anything other than Him for the blink of an eye.

When the soul is the opposite of this, it is the soul that commands evil. It commands its owner to what it desires: the lusts of error and the following of falsehood. It is the abode of every evil, and if one obeys it, it leads him to every ugliness and every abhorrence. Allah, may He be exalted, informed that it is "commanding evil," and He did not say "commanding" (only), because this is frequent from it, and it is its habit and its custom, except when Allah shows mercy to it and makes it pure, so that it commands its owner to good. That is from the mercy of Allah, not from the soul itself. For by its very nature it commands evil, because it was created in origin ignorant and wrongdoing, except for those whom Allah has mercied. Justice and knowledge come to it as something adventitious, through the inspiration of its Lord and Originator who grants it that. When He does not inspire it with its right guidance, it remains in its wrongdoing and its ignorance. It was not commanding except in accordance with the requirement of ignorance and wrongdoing. Thus, were it not for the grace and mercy of Allah upon the believers, not a single soul among them would have been purified.

When Allah, may He be glorified, wills good for it, He places in it what purifies and reforms it, from intentions and perceptions. When He does not will that for it, He leaves it in the state in which it was created, of ignorance and wrongdoing.

The cause of wrongdoing is either ignorance or need. The soul is originally ignorant, and need is inseparable from it. Therefore its commanding of evil is inseparable from it unless the mercy and bounty of Allah reach it.

From this it is known that the servant's need of his Lord is above every need, and no need is comparable to it by which it could be measured. For if He withholds from him His mercy, His guidance and His direction for the blink of an eye, he is lost and destroyed.

(Section)

As for the self-reproaching soul (al-lawwamah), there is disagreement regarding the derivation of this word: is it from taluwwum, which is changing and wavering, or is it from al-lawm (blame)? The expressions of the early generations (al-salaf) revolve around these two meanings.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "I said to Ibn 'Abbas: 'What is the lawwamah?' He said: 'It is the base soul (al-nafs al-la'imah).'"
Mujahid said: "It is the one that regrets what has passed and blames itself for it."
Qatadah said: "It is the immoral (al-fajirah)."
'Ikrimah said: "It blames for good and evil."
'Ata' said, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Every soul will blame itself on the Day of Resurrection. The one who did good will blame himself that he did not increase in goodness, and the one who did evil will blame himself that he did not turn back from his evil."
Al-Hasan said: "The believer, by Allah, you see him only blaming himself in all his states. He considers himself deficient in everything he does, so he regrets and blames himself. As for the immoral, he goes on heedlessly and does not reproach himself."

These are the expressions of those who held that it is from blame.

As for those who derived it from taluwwum, it is because of its frequent wavering and self-blame, and because it does not remain in one state.

The first is more evident, for if this latter meaning were intended, it would be said "al-mutalawwimah," just as one says "al-mutalawwinah" and "al-mutaraddidah." But wavering is among the necessary consequences of the first view, for because of its self-blame and its lack of steadfastness, it does a thing and then blames itself for it. So wavering is a necessary consequence of blaming.

The soul may at one time be commanding, at another self-reproaching, and at another tranquil. Indeed, within a single day and a single hour, both this and that occur in it. The ruling follows what predominates in its states. Its being tranquil is an attribute of praise for it. Its being commanding evil is an attribute of blame for it. Its being self-reproaching is divided between praise and blame, according to what it blames itself for.

The purpose: to mention the treatment of the heart's disease through the domination of the commanding soul over it.

It has two treatments: holding it to account (muhasabah) and opposing it (mukhalafah). The heart is destroyed by neglecting its accountability, and by agreeing with it and following its desire. In the hadith narrated by Ahmad and others, on the authority of Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The intelligent (al-kays) is the one who holds himself to account (dana nafsahu) and works for what comes after death. The incapable (al-'ajiz) is the one who follows his soul's desires and wishes (tamanna) upon Allah." "Dana nafsahu" means: he called it to account (hasabaha).

Imam Ahmad mentioned from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Hold yourselves to account before you are held to account, and weigh yourselves before you are weighed, for it is easier for you on the Day of Reckoning to have held yourselves to account today, and adorn yourselves for the Greatest Presentation, the Day when you will be presented, and nothing of you will be hidden."

Ibn al-Qayyim also reported from al-Hasan who said: "You will not meet a believer except that he calls himself to account: 'What did you intend to do? What did you intend to eat? What did you intend to drink?' But the wicked person goes on heedlessly, never calling himself to account."

Qatadah said, regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and his affair was ruin﴾ [al-Kahf: 28].
He ruined himself and was defrauded. Yet you see him guarding his wealth while neglecting his religion.

Al-Hasan said: "A servant will remain in goodness as long as he has a preacher within himself, and his drive is accompanied by self-accounting."

Maymun ibn Mihran said: "A servant will not be pious until he is more strict in calling himself to account than a partner is with his partner. For this reason it has been said: the self is like a treacherous partner. If you do not hold it to account, it will take your wealth."

Maymun ibn Mihran also said: "The pious person is more strict in calling himself to account than a sinful ruler, and than a stingy partner."

Imam Ahmad reported from Wahb who said: "It is written in the wisdom of the family of Dawud: It is incumbent upon the intelligent person not to be heedless of four hours: an hour in which he confides in his Lord, an hour in which he calls his self to account, an hour in which he is alone with his brothers who inform him of his faults and speak the truth to him about himself, and an hour in which he leaves his self free to enjoy its pleasures in what is lawful and permissible, for in this hour there is help for those other hours and refreshment for the hearts." This has also been reported as a statement traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was narrated by Abu Hatim, Ibn Hibban and others.

Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays used to come to the lamp, place his finger in it, and then say: "Feel it, O Ahnaf! What made you do what you did on such-and-such a day? What made you do what you did on such-and-such a day?" And he would weep.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to some of his governors: "Call yourself to account in times of ease before you are called to account in times of hardship, for whoever calls himself to account in times of ease before he is called to account in times of hardship, his affair will end in contentment and happiness. And whoever is distracted by his life and occupied by his desires, his affair will end in regret and loss."

Al-Hasan said: "The believer is one who keeps his own self upright. He calls himself to account for the sake of Allah. The reckoning on the Day of Resurrection is only light for those who called themselves to account in this world, and it is only heavy on those who took this matter without self-accounting. The believer is surprised by something that pleases him and says: 'By Allah, I truly desire you, and you are indeed among my needs. But by Allah, there is no way to reach you. Far, far! You have been barred from me.' Then something slips from him and he returns to himself and says: 'What did I want with this? What is it to me? By Allah, I will never return to this again.' The believers are a people whom the Qur'an has held back and whom it has kept away from their ruin. The believer is a captive in this world, striving to free his neck. He feels no security in anything until he meets Allah. He knows that he will be held accountable for his hearing, his sight, his tongue and his limbs; he will be held accountable for all of that."

Malik ibn Dinar said: "May Allah have mercy on a servant who says to his self: 'Are you not the one who did such-and-such? Are you not the one who did such-and-such?' Then he restrains it, then bridles it, then binds it to the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it becomes its leader."

The self, in relation to its owner, has been compared to a partner in wealth. Just as the goal of a partnership, which is profit, is not achieved except by first making a stipulation regarding what the partner will do, then secondly by observing and supervising what he does and monitoring him, then thirdly by calling him to account, and fourthly by preventing him from treachery if he is found to be treacherous, likewise is the self. First, one makes a condition with it to guard the seven limbs, whose guarding is the capital, and the profit comes after that. Whoever has no capital, how can he hope for profit? These seven limbs, namely the eye, the ear, the mouth, the tongue, the private parts, the hand and the foot, are the vehicles of destruction and salvation. Some are destroyed through neglecting them and failing to guard them, and some are saved through guarding and observing them. Guarding them is the foundation of all good, and neglecting them is the foundation of all evil. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ [al-Nur: 30].
And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not walk on the earth arrogantly; indeed, you will never tear the earth apart, nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾ [al-Isra: 37]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all those one will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra: 36]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And tell My servants to speak that which is best﴾ [al-Isra: 53]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice﴾ [al-Ahzab: 70].
And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah; and let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾ [al-Hashr: 18].

When he stipulates with it to guard these limbs, he then moves on to observing them, supervising them and monitoring them, and he does not neglect them. For if he neglects them for a moment, they will certainly indulge in treachery. If he persists in neglect, they will persist in treachery until they consume the entire capital. Whenever he senses a shortfall, he moves on to self-accounting. Then the reality of profit and loss becomes clear to him. When he senses loss and is certain of it, he recovers from it what a partner recovers from his partner: by demanding repayment for what has passed, and by standing in guarding and monitoring in the future. He has no hope of dissolving the partnership with this treacherous one and replacing him with another, for he must have him. So he should strive to monitor and call him to account, and he should beware of neglecting him.

What helps him in this monitoring and self-accounting is his knowledge that whenever he strives in it today, he will find rest from it tomorrow when the reckoning passes to someone else; and whenever he neglects it today, the reckoning will become harder for him tomorrow.

What also helps him is his knowledge that the profit of this trade is dwelling in Paradise and looking at the Face of the Lord, the Glorified, and its loss is entering the Fire and being veiled from the Lord, the Exalted. When he is certain of this, self-accounting becomes easy for him today. It is therefore incumbent upon the prudent believer who believes in Allah and the Last Day not to neglect calling his self to account and restricting it in its movements, its rests, its thoughts and its steps. Every breath of life is a precious jewel with no equal, by which a treasure can be bought whose bliss never ends, for all eternity. Wasting these breaths, or selling them for what brings about one's own destruction, is a great loss, and none would permit such a thing except the most ignorant, foolish and least intelligent of people. The reality of this loss will only become clear to him on the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a great distance﴾ [Al ʿImran: 30].

(Section)
Self-accounting is of two kinds: one kind before the action, and one kind after it.

As for the first kind, it is that a person stops at the first stirring of his intention and will, and does not rush into action until it becomes clear to him that it outweighs leaving it.

Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "May Allah have mercy on a servant who stops at his intention. If it is for Allah, he proceeds; if it is for other than Allah, he holds back."

Some have explained this, saying: When the self is moved toward some action and the servant resolves upon it, he first stops and considers whether that action is within his capacity or beyond it and not achievable. If it is not within his capacity, he does not proceed with it. If it is within his capacity, he stops a second time and considers whether doing it is better for him than leaving it, or leaving it is better for him than doing it. If it is the latter, he leaves it and does not proceed. If it is the former, he stops a third time and considers whether the motive behind it is the desire for the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and His reward, or the desire for status, praise and wealth from creation. If it is the latter, he does not proceed; and if it leads him to his goal, this is so that the self does not become accustomed to shirk, and so that acting for other than Allah becomes light for it. The more that becomes light for it, the heavier acting for Allah becomes upon it, until it becomes the heaviest thing for it. If it is the former, he stops a fourth time and considers whether he has helpers who assist him and support him, if the action requires that, or not. If he has no helpers, he refrains from it, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) refrained from fighting in Makkah until he had strength and supporters. If he finds that he is assisted in it, he should proceed, for he will be supported. Success is only lost by one who misses one of these qualities; but when they are all present, success is not lost.

These are four stages in which a person needs to call his self to account before the act. Not everything a servant wants to do is within his capacity, not everything within his capacity is better for him to do than leave, not everything better for him to do than leave is done for Allah, and not everything done for Allah is assisted. When he calls himself to account on these matters, what he should proceed with and what he should refrain from becomes clear to him.

(Section)
The second kind is calling the self to account after the action. It has three types.

The first: calling the self to account for an act of obedience in which it fell short regarding Allah's right, so that it did not perform it in the manner it should have been performed.
Allah's right in obedience consists of six matters, which have already been mentioned: sincerity in the action, advising Allah in it, following the Messenger in it, witnessing the station of excellence (ihsan) in it, witnessing Allah's favour upon him in it, and witnessing one's own shortcoming in it after all of that.
So he calls himself to account: Has it fulfilled these stations their due? Did he bring them into this act of obedience?

The second: that he calls himself to account for every action whose abandonment would have been better for him than doing it.

The third: that he calls himself to account for a permissible or customary matter: why did he do it? Did he intend by it Allah and the Last Abode? Then he is profiting. Or did he intend by it the world and its immediate gains? Then he loses that profit and misses out on attaining it.

(Section)
The most harmful thing for him is neglect, abandoning self-accounting, being carried away, making matters easy and letting them run their course. For this leads a person to destruction. This is the state of the deluded: they close their eyes to the consequences, let their affairs drift, rely on pardon, neglect calling their self to account, and disregard consideration of the outcome. When a person does this, transgressions become easy for him and he becomes familiar with them, and weaning himself from them becomes difficult. Had his sound judgement been present, he would have known that restraint is easier than weaning oneself away from what one has become accustomed to and used to.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: "A man from Quraysh told me, claiming that he was a descendant of Talhah ibn ʿUbayd Allah, said: Tawbah ibn al-Summah was at al-Raqqah, and he was one who called himself to account. One day he took account, and he found that he was sixty years old. He then counted his days, and they came to twenty-one thousand and five hundred days. He cried out and said: 'Woe is me! Shall I meet my Lord with twenty-one thousand sins? How, when every day has thousands of sins?' Then he fell unconscious, and he was dead. They heard a speaker say: 'How swift a rush to the highest Paradise!'"

The summary of this is: he should first call his self to account regarding the obligatory duties, and if he finds some shortfall in them, he should make it up, either by making up what was missed or by correcting it. Then he should call it to account regarding the prohibitions, and if he knows that he committed any of them, he should make amends through repentance, seeking forgiveness, and good deeds that wipe out sins. Then he should call his self to account for heedlessness. If he has been heedless of what he was created for, he should make up for it through remembrance and turning to Allah, the Exalted. Then he should call it to account for what he has said, or what his feet have walked toward, or what his hands have seized, or what his ears have heard: What did he intend by this? Why did he do it? In what manner did he do it? He should know that for every movement and word of his, two records will be unfolded: one recording why he did it, and one recording how he did it. The first is a question about sincerity, and the second is a question about following the Sunnah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr: 92–93].
And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers. Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, for We were not absent﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 6–7].
And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That He may question the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ahzab: 8].
If the truthful are questioned and held accountable for their truthfulness, then what is to be expected for the liars?

Muqatil said: "Allah the Exalted says: We took their covenant so that Allah may question the truthful, meaning the prophets, about conveying the message." Mujahid said: "He questions those who convey and deliver from the messengers, that is, whether they conveyed from them as the messengers themselves are questioned, whether they conveyed from Allah, the Exalted."

The correct view is that the verse encompasses both of these meanings. The truthful are the messengers, and those who convey from them. The messengers are questioned about conveying their messages, and those who convey from them are questioned about conveying what the messengers conveyed to them. Then those to whom the message was delivered are questioned about how they answered the messengers, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says: "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65].

Qatadah said: "There are two words about which the first and the last will be questioned: 'What were you worshipping?' and 'What did you answer the messengers?' So He questions about the one worshipped and about the worship."

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about pleasure﴾ [al-Takathur: 8].
Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "Allah the Exalted says: Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will surely question you about the bounty you enjoyed in this world: What did you do with it? From where did you obtain it? On what did you spend it? And what did you do with it?"
Qatadah said: "Allah questions every servant about what He entrusted to him of His favour and His right."

The bounty about which one is questioned is of two kinds: one kind is obtained lawfully and spent in its rightful place, and one is questioned about giving thanks for it. The other kind is obtained unlawfully and spent in the wrong place, and one is questioned about how it was acquired and how it was spent.

Since the servant is questioned and called to account for everything, even for his hearing, his sight and his heart, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, about all of those one will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra: 36], he is entitled to call his self to account before the reckoning is scrutinized.

The obligation of self-accounting is indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah; and let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾ [al-Hashr: 18].
Allah the Exalted says: Let each of you look at what deeds he has sent ahead for the Day of Resurrection: Are they among the righteous deeds that will save him, or among the evil deeds that will destroy him?
Qatadah said: "Your Lord has continued to bring the Hour closer until He made it like tomorrow."
The point is that the heart's soundness comes through self-accounting, and its corruption comes through neglecting it and being carried away with it.

(Section)
There are many benefits in calling the self to account. Among them: becoming aware of its faults. Whoever is not aware of his own fault cannot remove it. When he becomes aware of its fault, he detests it for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.

Imam Ahmad reported from Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man does not truly understand until he detests people for the sake of Allah, then returns to himself and detests himself even more."

Mutarrif ibn ʿAbd Allah said: "Were it not for what I know of myself, I would have hated people."

Musarrif said in his supplication at ʿArafah: "O Allah, do not reject people because of me."

Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani said: "When I looked at the people of ʿArafat, I thought that they had been forgiven, had it not been that I was among them."

Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani said: "When the righteous are mentioned, I am far removed from them."

When Sufyan al-Thawri was dying, Abu al-Ashhab and Hammad ibn Salamah entered upon him. Hammad said to him: "O Abu ʿAbd Allah, have you not been made safe from what you feared, and are you not going to meet the One whom you hope in, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful?" He said: "O Abu Salamah, do you hope that someone like me will be saved from the Fire?" He said: "Indeed, by Allah, I hope that for you."

Zayd narrated from Muslim ibn Saʿid al-Wasiti who said: Hammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Zayd informed me that his father told him: "We went out on a military campaign toward Kabul, and in the army was Silah ibn Ashyam. The people stopped at the time of ʿIshaʾ, prayed, and then he lay down. I said: 'I will certainly observe his deeds.' He waited for the people to become heedless, until I said: 'The eyes have become still,' then he rose and entered a thicket near us. I followed in his footsteps. He performed wudu, then stood to pray, and a lion came until it approached him. I climbed a tree and saw him turn, or perhaps he was counting cubs? When he prostrated, I said: 'Now it will tear him apart.' He sat, then ended his prayer with the salam and said: 'O beast, seek your sustenance from another place.' It turned away, and its roar was so loud that I thought the mountains would split from it. He continued praying like that until the time of Fajr, when he sat down, praised Allah with praises I had never heard the like of, and then said: 'O Allah, I ask You to protect me from the Fire, and someone like me is too humble to dare ask You for Paradise.' Then he returned, and in the morning he appeared as if he had spent the night on bedding, while I was in a state of exhaustion that only Allah knows."

Yunus ibn ʿUbayd said: "I find a hundred qualities of goodness, yet I know that in my self there is not even one of them."

Muhammad ibn Wasiʿ said: "If sins had a smell, no one could sit with me."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported from al-Khuld ibn Ayyub who said: "There was a monk among the Children of Israel who had been in a hermitage for sixty years. He was visited in a dream and told: 'So-and-so the cobbler is better than you,' night after night. So he went to the cobbler and asked him about his deeds. He said: 'I am a man who rarely passes by anyone without thinking that he is in Paradise while I am in the Fire.' So he was given preference over the monk because of his self-belittling."

Dawud al-Ta'i was mentioned in the presence of some rulers, and they praised him. He said: "If people knew some of what we are in, no tongue would ever be free to praise us."

Abu Hafs said: "Whoever does not suspect his own soul at all times, does not oppose it in every state, and does not steer it away from what it dislikes in all its times, is deluded. And whoever looks at it with approval for anything in it has destroyed it."

The soul calls to ruin, aids the enemies, aspires to every ugliness, and follows every evil. By its nature it runs in the field of opposition.

So the blessing that has no danger to it is to get out of the soul's control and free oneself from its bondage, for it is the greatest veil between the servant and Allah, Exalted. The one who knows it best is the one who most belittles it and abhors it.

Ibn Abi Hatim said in his tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis): Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Muqaddami narrated to us: Amir ibn Salih narrated to us, from his father, from Ibn Umar, that Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Allah, forgive me my wrongdoing and my disbelief." Someone said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is wrongdoing; what about disbelief?" He said: ﴿Indeed, man is a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

He said: Yunus ibn Habib narrated to us: Abu Dawud narrated to us, from al-Salt ibn Dinar: Uqba ibn Sahban al-Hunai narrated to us, who said: "I asked Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, about the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants; of them is one who wrongs himself, and of them is one who is moderate, and of them is one who outstrips in good deeds, by Allah's permission﴾ [Fatir: 32].

She said: "My son, these are all in Paradise. As for the one who outstrips in good deeds, he is the one who passed away in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bore witness of Paradise and provision. As for the moderate one, he is the one who followed their path from among his companions until he joined them. As for the one who wrongs himself, he is like me and you." Thus she placed herself among us.

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj narrated to us: Shurayk narrated to us, from Asim, from Abu Wa'il, from Masruq, who said: Abd al-Rahman entered upon Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, and she said:

"I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: 'Among my companions there are some who will not see me after I die, ever.'" So Abd al-Rahman left her in alarm until he entered upon Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He said to him: "Listen to what your mother says." So Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, stood up until he came to her, entered upon her and asked her. Then he said: "I beseech you by Allah, am I one of them?" She said: "No, and I will never absolve anyone after you."

I heard our shaykh say: "She only meant that I will not open this door for her, and she did not mean that you alone are free of that, apart from the rest of the Companions."

Abhorrence of the soul for the sake of Allah is among the attributes of the siddiqin (the truthful, sincere ones). A servant may draw closer to Allah, glorified is He, through it in a single moment by many times what he draws closer by action.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported from Malik ibn Dinar, who said: "A group of the Children of Israel were in their mosque on a day of festival. A young man came and stood at the door of the mosque and said: 'Someone like me does not enter with you. I am the owner of such and such, I am the owner of such and such,' belittling himself. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to their prophet: 'Indeed, so-and-so is a truthful one.'"

Imam Ahmad said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Anas narrated to us: Mundhir narrated to us, from Wahb: "A wandering worshipper worshipped Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for seventy years. Then one day he went out, belittled his deeds, complained to Allah, Exalted, about them, and confessed his sin. Then a messenger from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, came to him and said: 'Indeed, this sitting of yours is more beloved to Me than your deeds throughout the past years of your life.'"

Ahmad said: Abd al-Samad, Abu Hilal, narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: The Messiah, Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, said: "Ask me, for I am soft of heart and humble in my own eyes."

Ahmad also mentioned, from Abd Allah ibn Rabah al-Ansari, who said: "Dawud, peace be upon him, would look for the most despised person among the Children of Israel, sit among them, and then say: 'O Lord, a poor man among poor people.'"

He also mentioned, from Imran ibn Musa al-Qasir, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, where shall I seek You?" He said: "Seek Me among those whose hearts are broken, for I draw near to them every day by a fathom, and were it not so, they would collapse."

In the Kitab al-Zuhd (Book of Asceticism) of Imam Ahmad: "A man from the Children of Israel worshipped for sixty years in pursuit of a need, but did not attain it. He said to himself: 'By Allah, if there were any good in you, you would have attained your need.' Then he was visited in a dream and it was said to him: 'Did you see your belittling of yourself at that hour? It is better than your worship during those years.'"

Among the benefits of taking account of the soul is that through it one comes to know one's duty to Allah, Exalted. Whoever does not know Allah's right upon him, his worship will hardly benefit him, and it is of very little use.

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj narrated to us: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to us, from Wahb, who said: "It reached me that the Prophet of Allah, Musa, peace be upon him, passed by a man who was supplicating and humbling himself, and he said: 'O Lord, have mercy on him, for I have shown mercy to him.' Allah, Exalted, revealed to him: 'Even if he supplicates Me until his strength is exhausted, he will not be answered until he considers My right upon him.'"

Among the most beneficial things for the heart is for the servant to consider Allah's right upon him. This brings about in him abhorrence of his own soul and belittling of it, frees him from self-admiration and seeing his deeds as a merit, and opens for him the door of humility, lowliness and brokenness before Allah, and despair of himself, and that salvation is attained only through Allah's pardon, forgiveness and mercy. For His right is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, that He be remembered and not forgotten, and that He be thanked and not disbelieved.

Whoever considers this right that his Lord has over him knows with certain knowledge that he does not fulfill it as it should be fulfilled, and that nothing suffices him but pardon and forgiveness, and that if he were judged by his deeds, he would perish.

This is the place of reflection for the people of knowledge of Allah, Exalted, and of their own souls. This is what made them despair of themselves and hung all their hope on Allah's pardon and mercy.

When you contemplate the state of most people, you find them in the opposite condition: they consider their own rights against Allah, and do not consider Allah's right over them. From here they became cut off from Allah, and their hearts were veiled from knowing Him, loving Him, longing to meet Him, and delighting in His remembrance. This is the utmost of a human being's ignorance of his Lord and of himself.

So taking account of the soul is the servant's consideration of Allah's right over him first, and then his consideration of whether he has fulfilled it as it should be fulfilled, second. The best of reflection is reflection on this, for it sends the heart journeying to Allah and casts it before Him, humbled, submissive, broken in a brokenness that contains its mending, and in need in a neediness that contains its richness, and abased in an abasement that contains its honor, even if it does whatever deeds it may. If he misses this, then what he has missed of righteousness is greater than what he has done.

Imam Ahmad said: Ibn al-Qasim narrated to us: Salih al-Madani narrated to us, from Abu Imran al-Jawni, from Abu al-Khalad, that Allah, Exalted, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him: "When you remember Me, remember Me while your limbs tremble, and be humble and tranquil at My remembrance. When you remember Me, let your tongue be behind your heart. When you stand before Me, stand in the station of a lowly, humble servant, and blame your soul, for it is more deserving of blame. And converse with Me when you converse with a heart full of awe and a truthful tongue."

(Among the benefits of a servant's consideration of Allah's right over him)

That it never lets him take pride in any deed at all, whatever it may be. Whoever takes pride in his deed does not ascend to Allah, Exalted. Imam Ahmad reported from one of the people of knowledge of Allah that a man said to him: "I stand in my prayer and weep until the plants almost grow from my tears." He said to him: "If you laugh while you confess your sin to Allah, it is better for you than to weep while you are proud of your deed, for the prayer of one who is self-admiring does not ascend above him." The man said: "Advise me." He said: "Upon you is abstinence from this world, and that you not dispute with its people. Be like the bee: if it eats, it eats what is good, and if it lays, it lays what is good, and if it lands on a branch, it neither harms nor breaks it. And I advise you to be sincere to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, like the dog's sincerity to its family: they starve it and drive it away, yet it refuses except to guard them and advise them."

From this, al-Shatibi took his saying:

It has been said: "Be like the dog, whom his family drives away, yet he does not cease, devoted, to advise them."

Imam Ahmad said: Sayyar narrated to us: Ja'far narrated to us: al-Jurayri narrated to us, who said: "It reached me that a man from the Children of Israel had a need with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He worshipped and exerted himself, then asked Allah, Exalted, for his need, but saw no success. So he spent the night belittling himself and said: 'O soul, why is your need not fulfilled?' He spent the night grieved, having belittled himself and blamed his soul. Then he said: 'By Allah, it did not come from my Lord, but it came from myself.' So he spent the night belittling himself and blaming his soul, and his need was fulfilled."

(Fa'idah – a benefit or note)

The secret of dropping the alif from interrogative "ma" when it follows a prepositional particle is that they wanted the wording to match the meaning. So they dropped the alif, because the sense of their saying "fīm" (فيم) is "in what thing are you eager?", "ilām" (إلام) is "to what thing are you heading?", and "hatām" (حتام) is "until what end will you keep on?", and similar.

They dropped the alif with the preposition, but did not drop it in the case of nasb (accusative) and raf' (nominative), so that the word would not be left on a single letter. When a preposition or a genitive-governing annexed noun is attached to it, it leans on that word, because the governing particle and the governed noun are like one word. Sometimes they also drop the alif in places other than the genitive position.

But if they drop the news (khabar), they say "mah yā Zayd" (مه يا زيد), meaning: "What is the news, and what is the matter?"

When the deletion in meaning became frequent, it became frequent in the wording too, but the hā' al-sakt (the silent hā', a pause-marker) is necessary so that one can stop on it.

From this is their saying "mahayim" (مهيم), the original being: "mā hādhā yā imraʾ" (ما هذا يا امرؤ, "what is this, O man?").

So they limited each word to one letter, and this is the utmost in brevity and deletion.

What encouraged them to do this was their being safe from ambiguity, since the situation of the one asked and the one asked about indicates the deleted element, so the addressee understands from "mahayim" what is understood from those four words.

A parallel to this is their saying "ayysh" (أيش) for "ayy shay'" (أي شيء, "what thing"), and "m Allāh" (م الله) for "yamīn Allāh" (يمين الله, "by God's oath").
